segments.title: HMS Dreadnought's 12-inch starting point
segments.summary: The guide uses HMS Dreadnought's 12-inch guns as the visual baseline for later battleship-calibre comparisons.
segments.body: The guide opens with a human reference: a head measured at roughly 10 inches from top to chin. HMS Dreadnought's 12-inch gun is then shown as a bore about one foot across. The comparison turns the calibre into a visible diameter rather than leaving it as a number. It establishes the scale used for every larger gun that follows.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces dreadnought gun calibres and identifies Dreadnought's 12-inch gun as the first comparison.

segments.title: The step from 12 to 13.5 and 14 inches
segments.summary: The Orion-class 13.5-inch gun shows that a seemingly modest increase in bore size still mattered in capital-ship armament.
segments.body: The Orion class supplies the 13.5-inch example. Set beside a 14-inch gun, the difference looks small, yet the transcript stresses that it is still enough to matter. This short comparison shows how half an inch can seem minor when viewed in isolation while remaining a real step in calibre. Opening here gives a direct visual bridge between the 12-inch starting point and the larger weapons that follow.

evidence.note: The transcript compares Orion's 13.5-inch gun with a 14-inch gun and says the difference still matters.

segments.title: Queen Elizabeth's 15-inch calibre
segments.summary: A chest-width comparison shows the diameter of the Queen Elizabeth class's 15-inch main battery.
segments.body: The Queen Elizabeth class introduces the 15-inch gun. Its shell width is compared with the width of a person's chest, turning the calibre into an immediate visual measure. The remark that it would hurt when it hit keeps the emphasis on projectile size rather than a detached number. This moment shows how much the bore has grown from Dreadnought's 12-inch starting point.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies the Queen Elizabeth class's 15-inch guns and compares the shell width with a chest.

segments.title: Colorado's 16-inch gun in human scale
segments.summary: The Colorado class's 16-inch guns push the visual comparison beyond a human head, illustrating the next jump in heavy-gun scale.
segments.body: The Colorado class provides the 16-inch example. The bore is large enough for the joke that two heads might fit inside it, continuing the human-scale comparison. The humor makes the extra inch beyond the Queen Elizabeth class's gun easy to picture. This is the last step before the guide reaches the 18-inch extreme.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies the Colorados' 16-inch guns and uses a two-head comparison for their diameter.

segments.title: HMS Furious, Yamato, and the 18-inch extreme
segments.summary: HMS Furious and Yamato close the guide's progression with a shoulder-width illustration of an 18-inch gun.
segments.body: The sequence ends with HMS Furious and Yamato as the 18-inch examples. The bore is shown as roughly shoulder width, the largest human-scale comparison in the guide. This visual completes the progression from Dreadnought's 12-inch gun to an 18-inch weapon. The final remark about the hit brings the sequence back to the physical size of the projectile.

evidence.note: The transcript names HMS Furious and Yamato as examples with 18-inch guns and compares the diameter with shoulder width.
